newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus missile purchase increases fears.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus missile purchase increases fears.

text.p: Cyprus's plans to buy Russian anti-aircraft missiles have increased fears of renewed conflict on the divided, heavily militarised island in a year which it was hoped would bring peace.

Fears have been expressed that a continuation of the arms build-up on Cyprus could derail United Nations-led efforts to reunite the island's Greek and Turkish Cypriots, separated by barbed wire for more than two decades.
The latest twist to the dispute are disclosures the Cypriot government plans to purchase the S-300 anti-aircraft system, sparking bellicose reaction in Turkey and Western concern.

On Thursday Turkey's state-run Anatalian news agency said Ankara was seriously considering a strike against the missile launchers "if Turkey's warnings to the Greek Cypriot administration are not heeded".
Anatolian quoted Defence Minister Turhan Tayan as saying that Turkey would use all possible means to halt the planned deployment.
"These threats from Turkey are nothing new," said Cypriot government spokesman Yiannakis Cassoulides earlier in the day. "We have heard such threats before."

Greece too shrugged off Turkey's warnings. Prime Minister Costas Simitis said Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides would be invited to Athens for talks on the issue this month, but added there was no concern that a new crisis would erupt between Greece and Turkey.

Ankara has warned the Greek Cypriots it will not tolerate a change in the military balance in the region. Nicosia is refusing to budge, saying the missiles are purely defensive to protect the southern Greek Cypriot populated areas of the eastern Mediterranean holiday island from a Turkish air raid.
"It is a tactic to get world attention but it is a very dangerous tactic," said one diplomat based in the divided capital Nicosia.
"This (missile purchase) raises the stakes for some nasty business but talk of war is probably pushing it a bit far," he said.

Turkey invaded northern Cyprus in 1974 in response to a short-lived coup engineered by the military ruling in Greece at the time. Both countries, with Britain, are guarantors of Cyprus's independence under a 1960 treaty.
Keeping the lid on the Cyprus conflict and Greek-Turkish tensions is seen as vital for wider stability in the Mediterranean and the Middle East.
NATO members but bitter rivals, Turkey and Greece nearly went to war last year because of a dispute about a tiny, uninhabited island in the eastern Aegean.
Greece is the Cypriot government's closest ally. It has a defence pact with Greek Cypriots and has warned Turkey a further advance south would mean war.
Earlier this week the United States openly criticised the Nicosia government for its purchase of the anti-aircraft system.
Greek Cypriot officials privately admit that part of their strategy is to up the military ante to re-focus international attention on Cyprus.
"It is obvious that a change in the military balance will have immediate repercussions on political behaviour," one Greek Cypriot official told Reuters.

Earlier this week U.S. Secretary of State-designate Madeleine Albright said Washington was prepared to play a heightened role in solving the Cyprus problem - but said all parties involved should take steps to reduce tension.
Underlying the need for a settlement, four Greek Cypriots and one Turkish Cypriot were killed in clashes along the U.N. manned buffer zone from June to October 1996 in the worst violence since 1974.

"Our role and our effectiveness will be influenced heavily by the parties' desire for our assistance and by their commitment to achieve a peaceful resolution of differences," Albright told the Senate.
Diplomats say the S-300, with a range of 150 km (90 miles), could knock out planes in Turkish air space.
Greek Cypriots have accused critics of not showing the same sensitivity to the build-up in the Turkish-occupied north which they say is armed with U.S weapons.

"When Turkish reconnaissance planes were flying all over Cyprus photographing everything I didn't see anyone in London or Washington complaining," Cypriot Foreign Minister Alecos Michaelides told Reuters. "They just passively watched,"

Michaelides disagreed that the purchase aimed at attracting world attention. "This provides security for us... the Turks have an air base in Lefkoniko (northern Cyprus) and the mainland is 40 miles away. If they attack we are stranded."

Northern Cyprus is one of the most densely militarised areas of the world, according to the United Nations. The 11,500 strong Greek Cypriot national guard in the south is weaker than the 30,000 Turkish forces in the north, but is engaged in a comprehensive programme to upgrade its defence capabilities.
